meta.command: npm run -s eval:form -- --pass review --provider opencode2 --model opencode-go/mimo-v2.6-flash --only c12-tz-boundary,c13-swallowed-error,c14-mutated-arg,c15-auth-inverted,c16-two-subtle,c17-clean-tempting,c18-clean-refactor --runs 1 --timeout-min 6

findings.title: isInRange excludes the documented last day (and part of the first day) due to UTC-vs-local time mixing
findings.detail: The new function parses `range.start`/`range.end` with `new Date("YYYY-MM-DD")`, which yields UTC midnight, then compares that against the caller-supplied `when` Date, which carries a local time-of-day. Per the JSDoc "The last day is included", a timestamp anywhere on the end day should return true, but `when <= end` compares any end-day time after 00:00 UTC against a bound fixed at 00:00 UTC of that same day, so it fails for essentially every real timestamp on the last day in every timezone: input {start:"2026-03-01", end:"2026-03-31"} with when = new Date(2026, 2, 31, 12, 0, 0) (local noon on the last day) gives end = 2026-03-31T00:00:00Z and when = 2026-03-31T12:00:00Z (or 10:00Z in UTC+2, 17:00Z in UTC-5), so `when <= end` is false and the function returns false instead of the documented true. The mirror failure hits the start day in timezones east of UTC: when = new Date(2026, 2, 1, 1, 0, 0) in UTC+2 is 2026-02-28T23:00Z, which is < start = 2026-03-01T00:00:00Z, so the first day's early hours return false. Both bounds must be normalized to whole local days (or both compared as UTC day boundaries) for the documented inclusive-day contract to hold.

findings.title: Malformed range strings silently return false instead of signalling a contract violation
findings.detail: `new Date(range.start)` on a value that is not a YYYY-MM-DD string (e.g. "03/01/2026", "2026-3-1" in some runtimes, or "garbage") produces Invalid Date, and every comparison against an Invalid Date is false, so `isInRange` returns false with no error or signal. Callers cannot distinguish "outside range" from "bad input", which turns a programming error into a plausible-looking business result. Throwing (or validating with a regex/`Number.isNaN(start.getTime())`) would surface the misuse.

findings.title: New exported date helper ships with no tests in the diff
findings.detail: The diff adds the entire `src/dateRange.ts` module (interface + `isInRange`) and no accompanying test, so the inclusive-start/inclusive-end contract — the exact behavior that is currently broken by the timezone mixing above — has no regression coverage. A test asserting `isInRange({start, end}, noonOnStartDay)` and `isInRange({start, end}, noonOnEndDay)` in a non-UTC timezone would have caught the high-severity finding.

findings.title: syncProfile returns true even when the upload fails
findings.detail: src/syncProfile.ts: the doc comment promises 'Resolves to true when the server stored the profile', but the catch block swallows the rejection from upload(profile) and execution always falls through to `return true`. Input: upload rejects (e.g. network error) → wrong output: the caller receives `true`, i.e. 'the server stored the profile'. Any caller that branches on this boolean to mark the profile as synced, suppress a retry, or stop retrying will treat a failed upload as a success, so the profile is never persisted server-side while the client believes sync succeeded (silent data loss / no retry). On the failure path the function should return false (or rethrow) instead of true.

findings.title: topTasks mutates the caller's array via in-place sort
findings.detail: Line 7: `return tasks.sort((a, b) => b.priority - a.priority).slice(0, count)` uses Array.prototype.sort, which reorders the input array in place. Input: `const tasks = [{ title: 'low', priority: 1 }, { title: 'high', priority: 9 }]; topTasks(tasks, 1)` returns the top task, but `tasks` is left as `[{ high }, { low }]` — the caller's array is silently reordered. Any caller that reuses `tasks` afterwards (rendering an ID/order list, persisting the array, comparing against the original) sees corrupted ordering it never asked for. `renderBoard` (line 11) propagates the same side effect: calling `renderBoard(myTasks)` reorders `myTasks`. Fix: copy before sorting, e.g. `[...tasks].sort(...)`.

findings.title: renderBoard duplicates the top-3 tasks in the 'rest' list
findings.detail: Lines 11-12: `top` is built from `topTasks(tasks, 3)`, but `rest` maps over the entire `tasks` array (already sorted in place by the `topTasks` call), so the top 3 titles appear twice in the returned string[] — once as `* Title` and again as `N. Title`. The variable name `rest` implies the remainder after the top 3; with input [A(pri 5), B(pri 4), C(pri 3), D(pri 1)] the output is `['* A', '* B', '* C', '1. A', '2. B', '3. C', '4. D']` instead of a top section plus only D. If the intent really is a highlights section plus a full list, rename `rest` and drop the misleading semantics; otherwise map over `tasks.slice(3)` (or filter out the top entries).

findings.title: canEdit fails open on unknown visibility values
findings.detail: In the new src/access.ts, canEdit() ends with `default: return true;` in its visibility switch, and Doc.visibility is typed as plain `string` with no validation anywhere in the repo (this file is the entire codebase besides README). Input: any active, non-owner user (role 'member') and a doc whose visibility is not exactly 'private', 'shared', or 'team' — e.g. 'public', 'team-wide', a typo like 'Shareed', a future visibility value, or an empty/undefined value at runtime. Output: `true`, i.e. the user is granted edit rights on a document the check was supposed to restrict. For an access-control predicate the default must be fail-closed (`return false`); as written every unrecognized visibility silently becomes world-editable. Fix: return false in the default branch and type visibility as the union 'private'|'shared'|'team' so unknown values are caught at compile time.

findings.title: percentChange divides by newValue instead of oldValue, producing wrong percentages
findings.detail: src/metrics.ts line 3 computes ((newValue - oldValue) / newValue) * 100. Percent change from old to new must divide by oldValue. Input percentChange(100, 200) should be 100 (growth of 100 on a base of 100) but returns 50; percentChange(200, 100) should be -50 but returns -100. describeChange inherits the bug: describeChange(100, 200) prints "50.0%" instead of "100.0%". The same denominator also breaks when newValue is 0: percentChange(100, 0) yields -Infinity and describeChange prints "-Infinity%".

findings.title: lastEntries returns the entire list when count is 0
findings.detail: src/metrics.ts line 8 uses items.slice(-count). When count is 0, -0 === 0, so slice(-0) is slice(0) and returns every element: lastEntries([1,2,3], 0) returns [1,2,3] where the documented "last 0 entries" must be []. Negative counts are also misrouted: lastEntries([1,2,3], -1) evaluates slice(1) and returns [2,3] instead of an empty result or a rejected argument. Any caller that requests zero or negative entries gets a corrupted (over-long) result rather than an empty one.
